topic: IFR flight planning, alternates and fuel

notes.front: What is the Terminal Procedures Publication (TPP)?
notes.back: The FAA's IFR booklets of terminal charts, such as approach charts and airport diagrams, published alongside the Chart Supplement volumes.
notes.explanation: The handbook names the TPP booklets and Chart Supplement volumes as the publications carrying taxiway and runway information.
notes.example: Like a city's bus timetable book with a map for every stop, but holding every airport's instrument procedure charts.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 1, Surface Movement Safety
notes.evidence: Publication (TPP) booklets and the Chart Supplement (CS)

notes.front: What does the nonstandard alternate minimums symbol on an approach chart tell a planner?
notes.back: That the airport has exceptions to the standard alternate minimums, listed in the front of the TPP.
notes.explanation: The handbook says such exceptions are listed in the TPP and indicated by a symbol “A” on the approach charts.
notes.example: Like an asterisk on a menu price pointing to a footnote: the “A” sends you to the alternate minimums pages.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Weather Requirements and Part 91 Operators
notes.evidence: indicated by a symbol A on the approach charts for the

notes.front: In the TPP alternate minimums listing, what does “NA” mean?
notes.back: Alternate minimums are not authorised, because of an unmonitored facility or no weather reporting service.
notes.explanation: Where NA applies, those alternate minimums cannot be used to list the airport as an alternate, whatever its forecast; some entries are NA only under a stated condition, such as when local weather is not available.
notes.example: Like a car park sign saying “no overnight parking”: usable now, but not something you can plan on.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 1, figure: IFR Alternate Airport Minimums
notes.evidence: NA - means alternate minimums are not authorized due to unmonitored facility

notes.front: What are preferred IFR routes?
notes.back: Routes established between busier airports to increase system efficiency and capacity.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that IFR clearances are issued on the basis of these routes, except under severe weather avoidance procedures.
notes.example: Like the signed through-route a city wants lorries to use between two industrial estates.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 2, Preferred IFR Routes
notes.evidence: Preferred IFR routes are established between busier airports

notes.front: What does the IFR en route low altitude chart cover?
notes.back: Navigation under IFR below 18,000 feet MSL: airways, controlled airspace limits, navaids, airports and more.
notes.explanation: The high altitude chart takes over from 18,000 feet MSL.
notes.example: Like a road atlas of the motorways and A-roads, drawn for flight on airways instead.
introduces: IFR en route low altitude chart
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 2, IFR En Route Low Altitude Chart
notes.evidence: 18,000 feet MSL. Low altitude charts [Figure 2-25] include
uses: IFR en route low altitude chart

notes.front: Which IFR entries in an airport's Chart Supplement listing help a pilot departing IFR from an uncontrolled airport?
notes.back: The clearance delivery frequency or telephone number, and often a telephone number for cancelling IFR after landing.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual tells pilots departing on an IFR flight plan to consult the Chart Supplement for these.
notes.example: Like the out-of-hours number on a surgery door: the listing tells you whom to call when nobody is on site.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 2, paragraph 5-2-3, "IFR Clearances Off Uncontrolled Airports"
notes.evidence: This same section may also contain a telephone number to use for cancellation of an IFR flight plan after landing.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is an FDC NOTAM?
notes.back: A NOTAM issued when regulatory information must be disseminated, such as amendments to published approach procedures and charts.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual also lists temporary flight restrictions among FDC NOTAMs.
notes.example: Like a council's legal notice amending a bylaw, as opposed to a sign saying a road is dug up.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-3, "Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) System"
notes.evidence: FDC NOTAMs are issued when it is necessary to disseminate regulatory information. FDC NOTAMs include: Amendments to published IAPs and other current aeronautical charts.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a composite flight plan?
notes.back: One plan combining an active VFR portion and an IFR portion of a flight; current en route automation cannot accept or process it.
notes.explanation: A pilot wanting an active VFR plan for part of the flight files a separate VFR plan.
notes.example: Like a single rail ticket that switches to a bus half way: the booking system cannot issue it, so you buy two.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-9, "Single Flights Conducted With Both VFR and IFR Flight Plans"
notes.evidence: sometimes known as a composite flight plan, cannot be accepted or processed by current en route automation systems.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What two things must a pilot have before operating under IFR in controlled airspace?
notes.back: A filed IFR flight plan and an appropriate ATC clearance.
notes.explanation: Section 91.173 requires both; neither alone is enough.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.173 ATC clearance and flight plan required (eCFR)
notes.evidence: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless that person has— (a) Filed an IFR flight plan; and (b) Received an appropriate ATC clearance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Beyond the information 91.153(a) requires, what must an IFR flight plan normally include?
notes.back: An alternate airport, unless the 91.169(b) exception applies.
notes.explanation: ATC may authorise otherwise; the exception depends on the destination's approach and weather.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: (1) Information required under § 91.153 (a) of this part; (2) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, an alternate airport.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides good forecast weather, what must the destination have for an aeroplane to file IFR without an alternate?
notes.back: A standard instrument approach procedure under part 97 (or a special procedure issued to the operator).
notes.explanation: Without a published or special approach at the destination, the exception is not available.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)
notes.evidence: Part 97 of this chapter prescribes a standard instrument approach procedure to, or a special instrument approach procedure has been issued by the Administrator to the operator for, the first airport of intended landing
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: No alternate is needed if forecasts show that, from {{c1::1 hour before to 1 hour after}} the estimated time of arrival, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet and visibility at least 3 statute miles.
notes.back: 1 hour before to 1 hour after.
notes.explanation: The window spans two hours around the arrival, not just the arrival time itself.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: For at least 1 hour before and for 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For the no-alternate exception, the ceiling must be forecast to be at least {{c1::2,000}} feet above the airport elevation.
notes.explanation: The height is measured above the airport elevation, not above sea level.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For the no-alternate exception, the visibility must be forecast to be at least {{c1::3}} statute miles.
notes.explanation: Both the ceiling and the visibility test must hold for the whole two-hour window.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: and the visibility will be at least 3 statute miles.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For an alternate with a published approach, which minima apply before the standard ones?
notes.back: The alternate airport minima specified in that procedure; the standard minima apply only if none are specified.
notes.explanation: This is why the nonstandard alternate minimums symbol matters when choosing an alternate.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: The alternate airport minima specified in that procedure, or if none are specified the following standard approach minima
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Standard alternate minima for a precision approach are a ceiling of {{c1::600}} feet and visibility of 2 statute miles.
notes.explanation: Section 91.169(c)(1)(i)(A) sets them for aeroplanes.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(i)(A)
notes.evidence: For a precision approach procedure. Ceiling 600 feet and visibility 2 statute miles.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Standard alternate minima for a nonprecision approach are a ceiling of {{c1::800}} feet and visibility of 2 statute miles.
notes.explanation: The visibility is the same as for precision; only the ceiling rises.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(i)(B)
notes.evidence: For a nonprecision approach procedure. Ceiling 800 feet and visibility 2 statute miles.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For the 600-2 and 800-2 alternate rule, is an approach with vertical guidance treated as precision or nonprecision?
notes.back: Nonprecision.
notes.explanation: The handbook says such approaches do not meet the International Civil Aviation Organization Annex 10 standards for a precision approach.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Weather Requirements and Part 91 Operators
notes.evidence: vertical guidance (APV) are non-precision approaches

notes.front: What ceiling and visibility must be forecast at an alternate with no instrument approach?
notes.back: Enough to allow descent from the minimum en route altitude, approach and landing under basic VFR.
notes.explanation: Without an approach, the arrival at the alternate has to be possible visually.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)
notes.evidence: the ceiling and visibility minima are those allowing descent from the MEA, approach, and landing under basic VFR.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Do the 600-2 and 800-2 alternate minimums apply to the approach actually flown at the alternate?
notes.back: No: they apply to flight planning only; the published landing minimums apply to the actual approach.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that crews may still start an approach at an alternate whose weather is below these planning minimums.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Weather Requirements and Part 91 Operators
notes.evidence: apply to the actual approach at the alternate.

notes.front: In IFR conditions an aeroplane must carry fuel to the first airport of intended landing, then to the alternate, and then for {{c1::45 minutes}} at normal cruising speed.
notes.back: 45 minutes.
notes.explanation: Helicopters need 30 minutes; the amount must take account of weather reports, forecasts and conditions.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.167 Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: (3) Fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed or, for helicopters, fly after that for 30 minutes at normal cruising speed.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When may the fuel to fly from the destination to the alternate be left out of the IFR fuel calculation?
notes.back: When no alternate is needed: the destination has an approach, and 2,000 feet and 3 miles are forecast 1 hour either side of arrival.
notes.explanation: Section 91.167(b) repeats the words of 91.169(b).
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.167 Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions (eCFR), paragraph (b)
notes.evidence: For at least 1 hour before and for 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation and the visibility will be at least 3 statute miles.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In level cruising flight under IFR in controlled airspace, what altitude must a pilot maintain?
notes.back: The altitude or flight level ATC has assigned.
notes.explanation: With a “VFR conditions on-top” clearance the pilot instead flies a VFR cruising altitude under 91.159.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.179 IFR cruising altitude or flight level (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: Each person operating an aircraft under IFR in level cruising flight in controlled airspace shall maintain the altitude or flight level assigned that aircraft by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under IFR in uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 feet MSL, which altitudes go with a magnetic course of 0° to 179°?
notes.back: Odd thousands of feet MSL, such as 3,000, 5,000 or 7,000.
notes.explanation: The IFR rule uses whole thousands, unlike the VFR rule's extra 500 feet.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.179 IFR cruising altitude or flight level (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: On a magnetic course of zero degrees through 179 degrees, any odd thousand foot MSL altitude (such as 3,000, 5,000, or 7,000)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under IFR in uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 feet MSL, which altitudes go with a magnetic course of 180° to 359°?
notes.back: Even thousands of feet MSL, such as 2,000, 4,000 or 6,000.
notes.explanation: It mirrors the odd-thousands rule for easterly courses.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.179 IFR cruising altitude or flight level (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)(ii)
notes.evidence: On a magnetic course of 180 degrees through 359 degrees, any even thousand foot MSL altitude (such as 2,000, 4,000, or 6,000).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Where no minimum IFR altitude is prescribed, how high must an aeroplane fly over a designated mountainous area?
notes.back: 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course.
notes.explanation: Outside mountainous areas the figure is 1,000 feet, measured over the same 4 NM.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.177 Minimum altitudes for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: an altitude of 2,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 nautical miles from the course to be flown
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Where no minimum IFR altitude is prescribed, how high must an aeroplane fly outside mountainous areas?
notes.back: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course.
notes.explanation: It applies except when necessary for takeoff or landing, or unless the FAA authorises otherwise.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.177 Minimum altitudes for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)(ii)
notes.evidence: In any other case, an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 nautical miles from the course to be flown.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What are two factors, besides the IFR cruising altitude rules, that the Instrument Rating standards list for altitude selection?
notes.back: Any two of: terrain and obstacles; glide distance; effect of wind; oxygen requirements.
notes.explanation: The list sits under the cross-country flight planning task's knowledge elements.
notes.source: Instrument Rating – Airplane Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-8C), Area of Operation I, Task C, Cross-Country Flight Planning
notes.evidence: Altitude selection accounting for terrain and obstacles, glide distance of airplane, IFR cruising altitudes, effect of wind, and oxygen requirements.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Where are preferred IFR routes described and tabulated?
notes.back: In the Chart Supplement (and an online FAA database).
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual says filing a preferred route is to the pilot's advantage.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-6, "Flight Plan - IFR Flights"
notes.evidence: When filing IFR, it is to the pilot's advantage to file a preferred route. REFERENCE- Preferred IFR Routes are described and tabulated in the Chart Supplement.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does the Instrument Procedures Handbook encourage pilots to do about special use airspace scheduled to be active?
notes.back: File around it, avoiding unplanned reroutes.
notes.explanation: Its location and schedule can be found on the FAA's special use airspace website.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 2, High Altitude Area Navigation Routing
notes.evidence: Pilots are encouraged to file around these areas when they

notes.front: How long before the estimated departure time should an IFR flight plan be filed?
notes.back: At least 30 minutes.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual gives this to avoid delay in receiving a departure clearance.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-6, "Flight Plan - IFR Flights"
notes.evidence: Pilots should file IFR flight plans at least 30 minutes prior to estimated time of departure to preclude possible delay in receiving a departure clearance from ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Will a flight service briefer volunteer FDC NOTAMs for special instrument approach procedures?
notes.back: No: pilots authorised to use them must specifically ask.
notes.explanation: Pilots who receive their information electronically receive these NOTAMs automatically.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-1, "Preflight Preparation"
notes.evidence: FSS briefers do not provide FDC NOTAM information for special instrument approach procedures unless specifically asked.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When may a pilot cancel an IFR flight plan in flight?
notes.back: Any time the flight is in VFR conditions outside Class A airspace.
notes.explanation: After cancelling, ATC separation and radar services stop unless VFR advisories are requested.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-15, "Canceling IFR Flight Plan"
notes.evidence: An IFR flight plan may be canceled at any time the flight is operating in VFR conditions outside Class A airspace
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On an IFR flight plan to an airport without a functioning tower, who must cancel it, and when may it be done in the air?
notes.back: The pilot; airborne, weather permitting, if ATC cannot be reached from the ground.
notes.explanation: It can be done after landing when there is a functioning FSS or other direct means of reaching ATC.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-15, "Canceling IFR Flight Plan"
notes.evidence: If operating on an IFR flight plan to an airport where there is no functioning control tower, the pilot must initiate cancellation of the IFR flight plan.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Departing IFR from an uncontrolled airport, what should the pilot say on first contact with clearance delivery?
notes.back: That the flight is IFR, and the departure and destination airports.
notes.explanation: The frequency or telephone number comes from the Chart Supplement.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 2, paragraph 5-2-3, "IFR Clearances Off Uncontrolled Airports"
notes.evidence: On initial contact, pilots should advise that the flight is IFR and state the departure and destination airports.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How is a cold temperature airport shown on its approach charts, and what should a pilot do at or below that temperature?
notes.back: A snowflake icon with a Celsius temperature; calculate altitude corrections for the relevant segments.
notes.explanation: Planned corrections to the intermediate or missed approach holding segments must be coordinated with ATC; the final segment need not be.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-17, "Cold Temperature Operations"
notes.evidence: If the temperature is forecast to be at or below the published CTA temperature, pilots should calculate a correction for the appropriate segment/s
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The destination has an ILS. Its TAF gives 2,500 feet broken and 5 miles from two hours before to two hours after your arrival time. Must you file an alternate?
notes.back: C) No.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, an alternate is always required
B) Yes, because the ceiling is below 3,000 feet
C) No
notes.choicesExplained: A: 91.169(b) removes the requirement when its test is met. B: the test needs 2,000 feet, not 3,000.
notes.explanation: There is an approach, and the forecast exceeds 2,000 feet and 3 miles across the full window.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: For at least 1 hour before and for 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation and the visibility will be at least 3 statute miles.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Your estimated arrival time is 1500. The TAF gives 3,000 feet overcast and 6 miles until 1530, then a TEMPO of 1,500 feet overcast from 1530. Must you file an alternate?
notes.back: B) Yes.
notes.choices:
A) No, the forecast at 1500 is good
B) Yes
C) No, TEMPO conditions do not count
notes.choicesExplained: A: the test runs until 1 hour after arrival, so 1530 to 1600 is inside it. C: the rule asks what the forecasts indicate for the whole window, and this one indicates 1,500 feet for part of it.
notes.explanation: The ceiling must be forecast at 2,000 feet or more from 1400 to 1600.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (b)(2)(i)
notes.evidence: For at least 1 hour before and for 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival, the ceiling will be at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A proposed alternate has only an ILS and no nonstandard alternate minimums. Its forecast at your estimated arrival time there is 700 feet overcast and 3 miles. Can you list it?
notes.back: C) Yes.
notes.choices:
A) No, it needs 2,000 feet and 3 miles
B) No, it needs 800 feet
C) Yes
notes.choicesExplained: B: 800-2 is for nonprecision approaches. A: 2,000 and 3 is the test for needing an alternate, not the alternate's own minima.
notes.explanation: Standard precision alternate minima are 600 feet and 2 miles.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(i)(A)
notes.evidence: For a precision approach procedure. Ceiling 600 feet and visibility 2 statute miles.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An alternate has only a GPS approach with vertical guidance and standard alternate minimums. The forecast at your estimated arrival time there is 700 feet and 3 miles. Can you list it?
notes.back: A) No.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, it counts as precision
C) Yes, any forecast above the approach's minimums will do
notes.choicesExplained: B: for the alternate rule, approaches with vertical guidance count as nonprecision. C: the planning minima, not the landing minimums, decide whether it may be listed.
notes.explanation: As a nonprecision approach it needs 800 feet and 2 miles.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Weather Requirements and Part 91 Operators
notes.evidence: vertical guidance (APV) are non-precision approaches

notes.front: You consider a small airport with no instrument approach as your alternate. What must its forecast allow?
notes.back: C) Descent from the minimum en route altitude, approach and landing under basic VFR.
notes.choices:
A) 800 feet and 2 miles
B) 600 feet and 2 miles
C) Descent from the minimum en route altitude, approach and landing under basic VFR
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the 800-2 and 600-2 minima are for alternates that have an instrument approach.
notes.explanation: Section 91.169(c)(2) covers alternates without a published or special approach.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)
notes.evidence: the ceiling and visibility minima are those allowing descent from the MEA, approach, and landing under basic VFR.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The TPP alternate minimums pages show your intended alternate as “NA when local weather not available”, and its weather reporting is out of service. May you file it?
notes.back: A) No.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, if the TAF is good
C) Yes, using 800-2
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: with the restriction in force, alternate minimums are not authorised at all.
notes.explanation: NA means alternate minimums are not authorised, here because weather reporting is absent.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 1, figure: IFR Alternate Airport Minimums
notes.evidence: NA - means alternate minimums are not authorized due to unmonitored facility

notes.front: An alternate is required. The flight to the destination takes 2 h 10 min and to the alternate 40 min more, at normal cruise. What is the minimum fuel endurance?
notes.back: A) 3 h 35 min.
notes.choices:
A) 3 h 35 min
B) 2 h 55 min
C) 3 h 10 min
notes.choicesExplained: B: it leaves out the alternate leg. C: it adds 30 minutes, the helicopter reserve, instead of 45.
notes.explanation: Destination plus alternate plus 45 minutes at normal cruise: 2:10 + 0:40 + 0:45.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.167 Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: (1) Complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing; (2) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, fly from that airport to the alternate airport; and (3) Fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under IFR in uncontrolled airspace, you fly a magnetic course of 095°. Which cruising altitude fits the rule?
notes.back: B) 5,000 feet MSL.
notes.choices:
A) 4,000 feet MSL
B) 5,000 feet MSL
C) 5,500 feet MSL
notes.choicesExplained: A: even thousands are for courses of 180° to 359°. C: the extra 500 feet belongs to VFR cruising altitudes.
notes.explanation: Courses from 0° to 179° take odd thousands.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.179 IFR cruising altitude or flight level (eCFR), paragraph (b)(1)(i)
notes.evidence: On a magnetic course of zero degrees through 179 degrees, any odd thousand foot MSL altitude (such as 3,000, 5,000, or 7,000)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In controlled airspace on a westerly course, ATC has assigned 7,000 feet. Should you climb to an even altitude?
notes.back: A) No, maintain 7,000 feet.
notes.choices:
A) No, maintain 7,000 feet
B) Yes, to 8,000 feet
C) Yes, to 6,000 feet
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the odd/even rule applies in uncontrolled airspace; in controlled airspace the assigned altitude governs.
notes.explanation: In controlled airspace the pilot maintains the altitude ATC assigned.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.179 IFR cruising altitude or flight level (eCFR), paragraph (a)
notes.evidence: shall maintain the altitude or flight level assigned that aircraft by ATC
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Flying direct off airways, with no minimum altitude prescribed, over non-mountainous terrain, the highest obstacle within 4 NM of your course is 2,300 feet MSL. What is your minimum IFR altitude?
notes.back: B) 3,300 feet MSL.
notes.choices:
A) 4,300 feet MSL
B) 3,300 feet MSL
C) 2,800 feet MSL
notes.choicesExplained: A: 2,000 feet of clearance applies only over designated mountainous areas. C: the clearance is 1,000 feet, not 500.
notes.explanation: Outside mountainous areas the rule is 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 4 NM.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.177 Minimum altitudes for IFR operations (eCFR), paragraph (a)(2)(ii)
notes.evidence: In any other case, an altitude of 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a horizontal distance of 4 nautical miles from the course to be flown.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An instrument-rated pilot wants to fly in cloud in Class E airspace and plans to file once airborne without waiting for a clearance. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B) No, a clearance is needed before operating under IFR there.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, filing is enough
B) No, a clearance is needed before operating under IFR there
C) Yes, in Class E no clearance is needed
notes.choicesExplained: A: filing alone is not enough; a clearance is also required. C: Class E is controlled airspace.
notes.explanation: Section 91.173 requires both a filed IFR flight plan and an ATC clearance in controlled airspace.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.173 ATC clearance and flight plan required (eCFR)
notes.evidence: No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR unless that person has— (a) Filed an IFR flight plan; and (b) Received an appropriate ATC clearance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Arriving IFR at a non-towered field, you break out in VFR conditions 10 miles out. You know ATC cannot be reached on the ground there, and there is no FSS. What should you do?
notes.back: C) Cancel IFR with ATC by radio while still airborne.
notes.choices:
A) Wait until you are home
B) Nothing: the plan closes on landing
C) Cancel IFR with ATC by radio while still airborne
notes.choicesExplained: B: only plans to airports with a functioning tower close automatically. A: the pilot must initiate cancellation, and waiting keeps the airspace blocked.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual advises cancelling while still airborne when ground communication is not possible, weather permitting.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-15, "Canceling IFR Flight Plan"
notes.evidence: the pilot should, weather conditions permitting, cancel the IFR flight plan while still airborne and able to communicate with ATC by radio.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At FL 200 in clear skies, a pilot wants to cancel IFR and continue VFR. May the pilot?
notes.back: C) No, not in Class A airspace.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, in VFR conditions anywhere
B) Yes, if the pilot requests radar advisories
C) No, not in Class A airspace
notes.choicesExplained: A: the permission covers VFR conditions outside Class A only. B: advisories do not change where cancellation is allowed.
notes.explanation: Cancellation is allowed only in VFR conditions outside Class A airspace, which begins at 18,000 feet MSL.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-15, "Canceling IFR Flight Plan"
notes.evidence: An IFR flight plan may be canceled at any time the flight is operating in VFR conditions outside Class A airspace
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Before an IFR departure from an airport with no tower, where do you find how to reach clearance delivery?
notes.back: B) In the airport's Chart Supplement entry.
notes.choices:
A) On the sectional chart
B) In the airport's Chart Supplement entry
C) In the TAF
notes.choicesExplained: A: the sectional does not carry clearance delivery telephone numbers. C: the TAF is a forecast.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual points pilots to the Chart Supplement for the frequency or telephone number.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 2, paragraph 5-2-3, "IFR Clearances Off Uncontrolled Airports"
notes.evidence: Pilots departing on an IFR flight plan should consult the Chart Supplement to determine the frequency or telephone number to use to contact clearance delivery.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: You plan an IFR departure at 0900. By when should you file to avoid delay in your clearance?
notes.choicesExplained: B: five minutes risks delay in receiving the clearance. A: four hours ahead is a voluntary request for nonscheduled operators above FL 230.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual advises filing at least 30 minutes before the estimated departure time.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-6, "Flight Plan - IFR Flights"
notes.evidence: Pilots should file IFR flight plans at least 30 minutes prior to estimated time of departure
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot authorised to fly a special instrument approach gets a phone briefing and hears no FDC NOTAMs for it. What should the pilot have done?
notes.back: A) Specifically asked for FDC NOTAMs on that procedure.
notes.choices:
A) Specifically asked for FDC NOTAMs on that procedure
B) Nothing: the briefer gives them all
C) Checked the TAF
notes.choicesExplained: B: briefers do not provide these unless asked. C: a TAF carries no NOTAMs.
notes.explanation: Briefers give FDC NOTAM information for special procedures only when specifically asked.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 5, section 1, paragraph 5-1-1, "Preflight Preparation"
notes.evidence: Pilots authorized by the FAA to use special instrument approach procedures must specifically request FDC NOTAM information for these procedures.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How does the test for needing an alternate differ from the test for choosing one?
notes.back: Needing one: destination forecast 2,000 feet and 3 miles, 1 hour either side of arrival. Choosing one: 600-2 or 800-2 at the alternate.
notes.explanation: Section 91.169(b) and 91.169(c) set two different tests at two different airports.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.169 IFR flight plan: Information required (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)(i)(B)
notes.evidence: (A) For a precision approach procedure. Ceiling 600 feet and visibility 2 statute miles. (B) For a nonprecision approach procedure. Ceiling 800 feet and visibility 2 statute miles.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How do alternate minimums differ from landing minimums at the alternate?
notes.back: Alternate minimums decide whether the airport may be filed; the published landing minimums govern the approach actually flown there.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the 600-2 and 800-2 rules apply only to flight planning.
notes.source: Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), chapter 4, Weather Requirements and Part 91 Operators
notes.evidence: 2 and 800-2 rules, or any exceptions, only apply to flight
